decision: deterministic coordination chain, parallel specialist fan-out, and QA review join
scope: lab orchestration and synthetic workers only
winner: coordination chain -> parallel specialists -> QA join

comparison.approach: coordination chain -> parallel specialists -> QA join
comparison.correctness: high: orchestrator/planner remain ordered, independent specialists share the same planning dependency, and QA cannot run until every selected specialist completes
comparison.robustness: high: uses existing durable MissionCoordinator dependencies and failure propagation without adding a second scheduler
comparison.latency: best safe critical-path latency when two or more specialists are selected because their execution overlaps
comparison.resourceUse: moderate: parallel workers may consume more CPU/RAM concurrently, bounded by selected agents and worker availability
comparison.regressionRisk: low-to-moderate: dependency graph generation changes, but queue, persistence, worker ownership, and planner routing contracts remain unchanged
comparison.qa: tests cover graph shape, concurrent specialist claims, QA join blocking, restart persistence/idempotency, and failed-specialist cancellation propagation

comparison.latency: worst for independent specialists because total latency grows approximately with the sum of specialist runtimes
comparison.qa: already covered by previous runtime tests

comparison.approach: full fan-out including orchestrator/planner and QA
comparison.correctness: low: specialists could execute before planning and QA could review incomplete outputs
comparison.robustness: low due to missing phase barriers

comparison.regressionRisk: high before current durable worker contracts are fully proven
comparison.qa: would require a new scheduler integration and distributed fault suite

whyItWon: It removes the largest avoidable orchestration latency while preserving deterministic phase ordering and reusing the durable queue's existing dependency and failure semantics. It adds no network service and no new persistence model.
failuresAndLessons: Parallelism improves wall-clock latency only when multiple specialists are selected and worker capacity exists; otherwise behavior approaches the serial baseline.
Peak CPU/RAM can rise because specialist work overlaps, so later benchmark gates should include worker-concurrency limits and resource telemetry.
QA is a hard join: one terminal specialist failure cancels QA through existing dependency propagation instead of reviewing an incomplete result set.
Submission idempotency remains derived per agent and assumes stable planner membership for a logical idempotency key.
This graph does not solve shared-snapshot multi-coordinator safety or prove a real Qubes boundary.
nextGate: run full Node QA on this head, then add a benchmark that compares serial-vs-fan-out critical-path latency and resource consumption under deterministic synthetic worker delays before Qubes activation
